models.collectorNote: Survivors are affordable pre-war motoring; the sixes are the usable ones. Condition and completeness beat rarity here, trim for these cars is not reproduced.

generations.name: Essex Four / Super Six
generations.note: Launched as a four, the Essex became a six in 1924 and one of America's best-selling cars. The line closed in 1932, succeeded by the Terraplane.

models.intro: Hudson's budget line that outsold its parent: the Essex made closed cars affordable, put a six-cylinder engine in reach of ordinary buyers, and carried Hudson through the 1920s. The Super Six name above it said everything about the formula, more cylinders, less money.
models.name: Essex

models.collectorNote: The utility coupe, a car that converts to a pickup, is the collector's favourite. Pre-war eight-cylinder cars are the rare ones.

generations.name: Terraplane / Hudson Terraplane
generations.note: The eight-cylinder Terraplane of 1933 was among the fastest cheap cars in America. Orville Wright bought one of the first. Post-war cars ran to 1947 as the Super Six line took over.

models.intro: Launched off the Essex County Airport runway in 1932, the name is the point, the Terraplane was Hudson's volume fighter: steel-bodied, quick for its price, and famous enough that bluesman Robert Johnson sang about one. It became simply 'Hudson' after 1938.
models.name: Terraplane

models.collectorNote: Oddball charm and genuine rarity keep Jet values honest rather than high; Twin H cars are the ones to chase.

generations.name: Jet / Jet-Liner
generations.note: The 202 cu in six came with the Twin H-Power twin-carburettor option at 114 hp, strong specific output for a 1953 compact. Just over 35,000 Jets were built across two years.

models.intro: Hudson's compact gamble: a small, tall, well-equipped sedan launched into the teeth of the horsepower war. It was a good car in the wrong year, and its development cost is part of why Hudson merged into AMC in 1954.
models.name: Jet

models.collectorNote: First-generation Twin H cars with racing provenance sit at the top; documentation matters, as tribute cars abound. The step-down structure rusts from the inside, inspect the perimeter frame rails.

generations.name: Hornet (step-down)
generations.note: The 308 cu in six was the largest six in American production. With the Twin H-Power twin carburettors it reached up to 170 hp, and Hornets won 27 of 34 NASCAR Grand National races in 1952.

generations.name: Hornet (AMC era)
generations.note: Built by AMC after the 1954 merger, the restyled 'Hash' Hornet kept the six, then took V8 power, a Packard-built V8 in 1956 and AMC's own 327 in 1957, the final year of the Hudson name.

models.intro: The step-down Hudson at its peak: a low, unit-body sedan whose big six humiliated V8s on the early NASCAR circuit, 'Fabulous Hudson Hornet' was a results sheet before it was a cartoon. The last true Hudsons before the AMC years turned it into a badge.
models.name: Hornet
